explanation: Has 12g added sugar (40% daily limit) and low fiber. Marketed as healthy but nutritionally similar to a cookie.
tip: Products with 'nature' in the name aren't always nutritious. Check the sugar content!

explanation: Contains 39g of sugar per can - that's nearly 10 teaspoons! Zero nutritional value beyond empty calories.
tip: Regular soda is one of the biggest sources of added sugar in American diets.

explanation: High protein (18g per serving), zero added sugar, minimal ingredients. An excellent choice for a healthy snack.
tip: Plain Greek yogurt is much healthier than flavored versions - add your own fruit!

explanation: Contains 27g of sugar per bottle - only slightly better than soda. The vitamins don't offset the sugar content.
tip: Marketing trick: 'Vitamin Water' sounds healthy but it's basically sugar water with added vitamins.

explanation: High in sodium (210mg per serving), unhealthy fats, and artificial ingredients. Low nutritional value.
tip: Chips are okay as an occasional treat, but shouldn't be a regular snack.

explanation: Good ingredients (nuts, minimal processing) but calorie-dense at 200 calories. Better than candy bars but not low-calorie.
tip: Nut-based bars are nutritious but watch portions - they're high in calories from healthy fats.

explanation: Decent fiber (3g) and whole grain, but still processed. Better than sugary cereals but not as nutritious as oatmeal.
tip: Look for cereals with at least 3g fiber and under 6g sugar per serving.

explanation: 30g of sugar per serving (2 pastries), highly processed, artificial colors. Basically frosted cake for breakfast.
tip: Pop-Tarts have more sugar than most desserts. Not a good breakfast choice.

explanation: Contains fruit and veggies BUT has 53g of sugar per bottle and zero fiber. Drinking fruit removes the beneficial fiber.
tip: Smoothies sound healthy but lack fiber. Better to eat whole fruits and vegetables.

explanation: Excellent source of healthy fats, protein (6g per oz), fiber, and vitamin E. One of the best snack choices.
tip: Raw or dry roasted nuts without added salt/sugar are one of the healthiest snacks available.

explanation: Good for athletes during intense exercise (electrolytes + quick energy), but unnecessary sugar for most people. 34g sugar per bottle.
tip: Sports drinks are designed for athletes exercising over 1 hour. Most people just need water.

explanation: High in sugar (14g per 3 cookies), unhealthy fats, and heavily processed. Pure dessert with no nutritional benefit.
tip: Cookies are treats, not snacks. Enjoy occasionally but don't fool yourself into thinking they're food.

explanation: Good for endurance athletes (250 calories, 5g fiber, 9g protein) but too calorie-dense for a regular snack. Contains 21g sugar.
tip: Energy bars are designed for people who need quick calories during activity, not desk workers.

explanation: Low calorie (35 per serving), high in vitamin A and fiber. Perfect crunchy snack with no downsides.
tip: Non-starchy vegetables like carrots are 'free foods' - eat as much as you want!

explanation: Better than chips (only 39 calories per cup, whole grain) but still processed and easy to overeat. Marketing emphasizes 'skinny' but portions matter.
tip: 'Skinny' or 'lite' on packaging doesn't always mean healthy - check actual nutrition facts.

explanation: 27g sugar per can, high caffeine (80mg), and artificial ingredients. Linked to heart issues when consumed regularly.
tip: Energy drinks combine dangerous levels of caffeine with massive sugar. Stick to coffee or tea.

explanation: Contains 18g sugar (12g added) - nearly as much as ice cream! Some protein (5g) but heavily sweetened. Better than candy but not ideal.
tip: Flavored yogurts often have as much sugar as desserts. Choose plain and add fresh fruit.

explanation: Good protein (6g), calcium, low sugar, portable. A genuinely healthy and convenient snack.
tip: Part-skim mozzarella sticks are one of the best grab-and-go protein snacks.

explanation: Made with whole wheat (better than white flour crackers) but still processed with 230mg sodium per serving. Okay in moderation.
tip: Whole grain crackers are fine occasionally, but watch sodium and don't eat the whole box.

explanation: 27g sugar, 250 calories, unhealthy fats. It's candy - delicious but nutritionally empty.
tip: Candy bars are treats for special occasions, not everyday snacks. Plan them intentionally.

explanation: Made from chickpeas - high in protein (2g per 2 tbsp), fiber, and healthy fats. Great with veggies.
tip: Hummus is a nutrient-dense dip. Pair with carrots or cucumbers for a perfect snack.

explanation: Made from dehydrated potatoes, high sodium (135mg per serving), unhealthy fats. Engineered to be addictive.
tip: Pringles' uniform shape means they're not real potato chips - they're processed potato paste.

explanation: High protein (20g), low sugar (1g), but highly processed with many artificial ingredients and sugar alcohols. Good for specific goals but not 'whole food.'
tip: Protein bars can be useful tools but aren't as healthy as real food. Use strategically.

explanation: Extremely high sodium (1,580mg per package - 70% of daily limit!), fried noodles, artificial flavoring. Very low nutritional value.
tip: Instant ramen is one of the highest-sodium foods. If you eat it, use only half the flavor packet.

explanation: 'Organic' sounds healthy but these still have 8g sugar per serving and are processed crackers. Better than regular graham crackers but not nutritious.
tip: Organic junk food is still junk food. The organic label doesn't make cookies healthy.

explanation: Perfect protein (6g), healthy fats, vitamins, only 70 calories. One of nature's most complete foods.
tip: Eggs are incredibly nutritious and convenient. Prep a batch on Sunday for the week.

explanation: Marketed as healthy ('veggie!') but they're fried potato starch with vegetable powder for color. Not much better than regular chips.
tip: Just because it says 'veggie' doesn't mean it counts as eating vegetables. These are still fried snacks.

explanation: 46g sugar per bottle - more than Coke! Plus 54mg caffeine and artificial colors. One of the worst beverages.
tip: Mountain Dew has more sugar than almost any other soda. It's liquid candy with caffeine.

explanation: Ingredients: peanuts, salt. High protein (8g per 2 tbsp), healthy fats, no added sugar. Calorie-dense but nutritious.
tip: Choose peanut butter with only peanuts and salt in ingredients. Avoid added sugar and oils.

explanation: Very low calorie (35 per cake) but also very low nutrition. Basically puffed air. Fine as a vehicle for toppings but not filling alone.
tip: Rice cakes are nearly nutrition-free. Use them as a base for peanut butter or avocado.
